title: The gold ring (James 2:1–13)
hook: don't give the rich visitor the good seat and the poor one the floor

segments.voice: Yesterday, quick to hear, and your line was swift to hear, slow to speak. Did you manage that one slow breath before you answered? Day six hundred seventy-two.

Two people walk into a gathering at the same moment. One has a gold ring on his finger and fine clothes. The other is in shabby, dirty clothes. Watch where the eyes go. Watch who gets greeted first, who gets a chair, who gets a glance and a nod toward the back. Often nobody decides to do it. It just happens, in churches, restaurants, offices. James pictures it happening in the gatherings of early believers, and he paints it so sharply you can almost hear the scrape of the chairs.

In the King James Bible: "For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment." And the greeters say to the rich man: "Sit thou here in a good place"; and to the poor man: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." Under my footstool. On the floor, by someone's feet. James calls it judging with evil thoughts. A small detail in the Greek: the word for assembly here is synagogue, the ordinary word for a gathering. Some readers take it as a sign of how close these believers were to synagogue life. Then James asks a question: "Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith?" The people you sent to the floor are the ones God honors. Then he reaches for what he calls the royal law, the king's law, from Leviticus: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Favoritism breaks it. You can't love your neighbor as yourself while assigning seats by the shine of their jewelry. And he ends with a short, startling line. Speak and act, he says, as people who will be judged by the law of liberty, because judgment will be without mercy to anyone who has shown no mercy. And then: "mercy rejoiceth against judgment." Modern versions say mercy triumphs over judgment. Picture a courtroom where mercy stands up and wins. The one who has shown mercy is met by it. This week we've moved from Philippians into James: rejoice always, whatever is lovely, contentment, count it all joy, every good gift, quick to hear, and now the gold ring.
screen: `GOD CHOSE THE POOR, RICH IN FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give the best seat away. Settle, and breathe. Picture the places you go in a normal week: a bus, a break room, a church, a family table, a group chat. In each one, who usually gets the good seat? Who ends up on the edge, quietly? Let one face come to mind, someone easy to overlook. Picture yourself making room for them: a chair pulled out, a question asked, your attention turned their way. Stay with that picture. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Synagogue. The ordinary Greek word for a gathering, the same word James uses for the believers' meeting: his picture of the rich man given the good seat, the poor man the floor.
Your line: mercy triumphs over judgment. Today, give the best seat, the first word or the full attention to the person who usually gets it last. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some churches read James 2:1–9 when training greeters and welcome teams, as a check on who gets noticed at the door.

fork.setup: you're greeting at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in dirty clothes arrive together. there's one good seat left. what does James say happens?
options: the poor man gets it, because he's more in need.

fork.reveal: "Sit thou here in a good place" to the rich, "sit here under my footstool" to the poor. James calls it judging with evil thoughts.

notes: The carry 'mercy triumphs over judgment' follows modern wording; the KJV of James 2:13 reads 'mercy rejoiceth against judgment'. Both are given.
συναγωγή in James 2:2 (εἰς συναγωγὴν ὑμῶν): confirm the framing as 'the ordinary word for a gathering' and the note about closeness to synagogue life.

The KJV quotation of 2:13 is a fragment of the verse; the first half is paraphrased.

Hook softened from 'James saw it happening' to 'James pictures it': 2:2 is framed as a hypothetical ('if there come'), and whether it reflects a real incident is debated. The letter's date and authorship are also debated, so 'this early letter' was changed to 'this letter'.

Editor review (y2 669–687 pass): 'many scholars' became 'some readers' for the synagogue note, and the myth reveal and trapdoor no longer state the letter's closeness to synagogue life as fact; hook's 'everywhere people gather' trimmed; unsourced howItsDone claim about congregations with no reserved seating cut.
